statement: If two medial straight lines commensurable in square only and containing a medial rectangle be added together, the whole is irrational; and let it be called a second bimedial straight line.
heath_proof: For let two medial straight lines AB, BC commensurable in square only and containing a medial rectangle be added together; I say that AC is irrational. For let a rational straight line DE be set out, and let the parallelogram DF equal to the square on AC be applied to DE, producing DG as breadth. [I. 44] Then, since the square on AC is equal to the squares on AB, BC and twice the rectangle AB, BC, [II. 4] let EH, equal to the squares on AB, BC, be applied to DE; therefore the remainder HF is equal to twice the rectangle AB, BC. And, since each of the straight lines AB, BC is medial, therefore the squares on AB, BC are also medial. But, by hypothesis, twice the rectangle AB, BC is also medial. And EH is equal to the squares on AB, BC,while FH is equal to twice the rectangle AB, BC; therefore each of the rectangle EH, HF is medial. And they are applied to the rational straight line DE; therefore each of the straight lines DH, HG is rational and incommensurable in length with DE. [X. 22] Since then AB is incommensurable in length with BC, and, as AB is to BC, so is the square on AB to the rectangle AB, BC, therefore the square on AB is incommensurable with the rectangle AB, BC. [X. 11] But the sum of the squares on AB, BC is commensurable with the square on AB, [X. 15] and twice the rectangle AB, BC is commensurable with the rectangle AB, BC. [X. 6] Therefore the sum of the squares on AB, BC is incommensurablewith twice the rectangle AB, BC. [X. 13] But EH is equal to the squares on AB, BC, and HF is equal to twice the rectangle AB, BC. Therefore EH is incommensurable with HF, so that DH is also incommensurable in length with HG. [VI. 1, X. 11] Therefore DH, HG are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; so that DG is irrational. [X. 36] But DE is rational; and the rectangle contained by an irrational and a rationalstraight line is irrational; [cf. X. 20] therefore the area DF is irrational, and the side of the square equal to it is irrational. [X. Def. 4] But AC is the side of the square equal to DF; therefore AC is irrational. And let it be called a second bimedial straight line.

10.38
**Statement:** If two medial straight lines commensurable in square only and containing a medial rectangle be added together, the whole is irrational; and let it be called a second bimedial straight line.

**Step 1.** Let AB, BC be two medial straight lines commensurable in square only (D10.1.2), containing a medial rectangle AB·BC, and let them be placed in a straight line so that AC is the whole. We must show that AC is irrational.

**Step 2.** Set out a rational straight line DE (D10.1.3). By 1.44 apply to DE a rectangle DF equal to the square on AC, producing DG as breadth; and by 1.44 apply to DE a rectangle EH equal to the sum of the squares on AB and BC, producing DH as breadth, so that H lies on DG.

**Step 3.** By 2.4, the square on AC equals the squares on AB, BC together with twice the rectangle AB·BC. Subtracting the equal areas EH and (sq AB + sq BC) from the equal areas DF and sq AC, the remainder HF equals twice the rectangle AB·BC (CN3); and HF is the rectangle contained by DE and HG.

**Step 4.** Since AB is medial, the square on AB is a medial area (10.21). Since AB, BC are commensurable in square, the squares on AB and BC are commensurable (D10.1.2); therefore their sum, the area EH, is commensurable with the square on AB (10.15). An area commensurable with a medial area is medial (10.23), so EH is medial.

**Step 5.** The rectangle AB·BC is medial by hypothesis. Twice this rectangle has to the rectangle itself the ratio 2 : 1, which a number has to a number, so twice the rectangle is commensurable with the rectangle (10.6). Hence HF, being twice the rectangle AB·BC, is medial (10.23).

**Step 6.** EH is a medial area applied to the rational straight line DE; therefore its breadth DH is rational and incommensurable in length with DE (10.22). Likewise HF is a medial area applied to DE, so HG is rational and incommensurable in length with DE (10.22).

**Step 7.** Since AB, BC are commensurable in square only, AB is incommensurable in length with BC. The square on AB and the rectangle AB·BC are parallelograms under the same height AB, so by 6.1, sq AB : rect AB·BC = AB : BC. Therefore the square on AB is incommensurable with the rectangle AB·BC (10.11).

**Step 8.** EH is commensurable with the square on AB (Step 4), and the square on AB is incommensurable with the rectangle AB·BC (Step 7); therefore EH is incommensurable with the rectangle AB·BC (10.13). Again, the rectangle AB·BC is commensurable with HF, its double (Step 5); therefore EH is incommensurable with HF (10.13).

**Step 9.** EH and HF are parallelograms under the same height DE with bases DH and HG, so by 6.1, EH : HF = DH : HG. Since EH is incommensurable with HF, DH is incommensurable in length with HG (10.11).

**Step 10.** Each of DH, HG is rational and incommensurable in length with DE (Step 6), hence commensurable in square only with DE; so the square on DH and the square on HG are each commensurable with the square on DE (D10.1.2), and therefore commensurable with one another (10.12). Thus DH, HG are rational straight lines commensurable in square but not in length, that is, commensurable in square only.

**Step 11.** Therefore DG, the sum of the two rational straight lines DH, HG commensurable in square only, is a binomial straight line and is irrational (10.36).

**Step 12.** DF is the rectangle contained by the rational straight line DE and the irrational straight line DG. If DF were a rational area, then, being applied to the rational straight line DE, it would produce as breadth a straight line rational and commensurable in length with DE (10.20); but its breadth DG is irrational. Therefore DF is not rational, that is, DF is an irrational area (D10.1.4).

**Step 13.** The square on AC is equal to DF and is therefore irrational; hence AC, the side of the square equal to this irrational area, is irrational (D10.1.4). Therefore the whole AC, composed of two medial straight lines commensurable in square only and containing a medial rectangle, is irrational; and let it be called a second bimedial straight line.
